extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent practitioners, and applicants prosecuting design patent applications
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and form-paragraph criteria for examining design patent applications, including obviousness/prior-art rejections (35 U.S.C. 102/103), and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112 (drawing disclosure, enablement, written description, and new matter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection over copending application with common inventor/assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is provisionally rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over the claim in copending Design Patent Application No. [1] which has a common [2] with the instant application. Based upon the different inventive entity and the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the copending application, it would constitute prior art if patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provisional rejection is based upon a presumption of future patenting of the conflicting application. Since the design claimed in the present application is not patentably distinct from the design claimed in the [4] application, this provisional rejection may be overcome by merging the two applications into a single continuation-in-part and abandoning the separate parent applications. For applications filed on or after November 29, 1999, this rejection might also be overcome by showing that the subject matter of the reference and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by the same person or subject to an obligation of assignment to the same person. See MPEP § 2146 et seq. Examiner notes: use this form paragraph when claimed design is obvious over design claimed in copending application that would qualify as prior art under pre-AIA 102(e) if published/patented; include a provisional nonstatutory double patenting rejection also; provide explanation of obviousness including differences and follow with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68; must be preceded by form paragraph 15.19.02.fti and, for certain priority situations, 15.10.15.

rubrics_metrics.name: 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2)/103 rejection - design disclosed, no common inventors or common assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being obvious over [1]. Because the reference names another inventor and has an earlier effectively filed date, it constitutes prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102(a)(2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the invention is not identically disclosed, if differences would have made the claimed invention obvious to a person of ordinary skill before the claimed effective filing date, it is unpatentable. This rejection might be overcome by: (1) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the subject matter disclosed in the copending application was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor or a joint inventor of this application (not prior art under 102(b)(2)(A)); (2) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing a certified priority document that satisfies enablement and description under 112(a); (3) perfecting the benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 by filing an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 with a specific reference under 1.78 and establishing the prior application satisfies 112(a); or (4) a showing under 37 CFR 1.130(b) of a prior public disclosure under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(B). Provide explanation of obviousness including differences. For certain priority claims, precede with form paragraphs 15.10.aia and 15.10.15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection - design disclosed but not claimed
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the reference, it constitutes prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph is used when the claimed design is obvious over subject matter disclosed in the drawings of an earlier-filed design or utility patent, or application publication, but is not claimed therein (e.g., disclosed in broken lines or as a subcombination). Since the claimed design is not the same as the invention claimed in the [3] patent, this rejection may be overcome by a showing under 37 CFR 1.132 that the design in the reference was derived from the designer of this application (not 'by another'), or by showing a date of invention prior to the reference's pre-AIA 102(e) date under 37 CFR 1.131(a). For applications filed on or after November 29, 1999, it might also be overcome by showing common ownership or obligation of assignment. In the Office action, insert the appropriate reference numbers and provide an explanation of obviousness including differences and follow with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection - design claimed in design patent with earlier prior art date and common assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over the claim in design patent [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the reference, it constitutes prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the design claimed in the present application is not patentably distinct from the design claimed in the [3] patent, this rejection may be overcome by submitting an oath or declaration under 37 CFR 1.131(c) stating that this application and the reference are currently owned by the same party and that the inventor named in this application is the prior inventor of the subject matter in the reference under 35 U.S.C. 104 (as in effect on March 15, 2013). In addition, a terminal disclaimer under 37 CFR 1.321(c) is required. A nonstatutory double patenting rejection must also be included in the action. Provide explanation of obviousness including differences and follow with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68. Precede by form paragraph 15.19.02.fti and, where applicable, 15.10.15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e)/103(a) rejection - design claimed in design patent with earlier prior art date and no common assignee
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being obvious over the claim in design patent [1]. Based upon the different inventive entity and the pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(e) date of the reference, it constitutes prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form paragraph when the claimed design is obvious over the design claimed in a design patent having an earlier prior art date under pre-AIA 102(e). In bracket 2, provide explanation of obviousness including differences and follow explanation with form paragraphs 15.70.fti and 15.67 or 15.68. For certain priority situations, precede with form paragraph 15.10.15.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection Maintained (15.38)
rubrics_metrics.description: The arguments presented have been carefully considered, but are not persuasive that the rejection of the claim under [1] should be withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, insert basis of rejection. Use when applicant's arguments do not overcome the asserted rejection(s).

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (single reference) (15.39.02)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is FINALLY REJECTED under 35 U.S.C. 103 over [1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, insert reference citation. See related form paragraphs in MPEP Chapter 700 for 'Action is Final' and 'Advisory after Final' paragraphs. Use appropriate wording where pre-AIA distinctions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rejection under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) (single reference) (15.39.02.fti)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is FINALLY REJECTED under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) over [1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description is incorporated into the claim by use of the language 'as shown and described.' See MPEP § 1503.01, subsection III. See form paragraphs in Chapter 700 for final action/advisory language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 (multiple references) (15.40.aia / 15.40.fti)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is FINALLY REJECTED under 35 U.S.C. 103 as being unpatentable over [1] in view of [2] (or pre-AIA equivalent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for final rejections based on combinations of references. See Chapter 700 form paragraphs for final action/advisory paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirements under 35 U.S.C. 112 (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention, and of the manner and process of making and using it, in such full, clear, concise, and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same, and shall set forth the best mode contemplated by the inventor or joint inventor. The specification shall conclude with one or more claims particularly pointing out and distinctly claiming the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin compliance analysis with determination of scope of protection sought by the claims (see In re Moore). For design applications, the drawing is incorporated into the claim by use of 'as shown' and 'and described.' If appearance/shape cannot be determined due to inadequate visual disclosure, rejection under 112(a) and (b) is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing incorporated into the claim; drawing adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: The drawing in a design application is incorporated into the claim by use of the claim language 'as shown.' Any determination of the scope of protection sought by the claim is also a determination of the subject matter that must be enabled by the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the appearance and shape/configuration of the design cannot be determined or understood due to an inadequate visual disclosure, the claim violates 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness) and 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (enablement). The drawing disclosure can be supplemented by narrative description (see MPEP § 1503.01, subsection II).

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of drawing detail depends on whether design is inherently 2D or 3D (Maatita principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some claimed designs are capable of being enabled and definite despite being disclosed using only a single plan- or planar-view. The level of detail required should be a function of whether the claimed design for the article is inherently two-dimensional (planar) or three-dimensional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Maatita permitted a single plan-view for a shoe bottom because the scope could be understood from that view. Conversely, inherently three-dimensional articles (e.g., entire shoe, teapot) could not be adequately disclosed with a single plan view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim scope limited to surfaces shown in full lines and written description
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of a claimed design is understood to be limited to those surfaces or portions of the article shown in the drawing in full lines in combination with any additional written description in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The title of the design identifies the article and may contribute to scope. It is assumed the claim was crafted to protect what the inventor regards as the invention. In absence of additional written disclosure, visible portions not shown are prima facie not part of the claim (see In re Zahn).

rubrics_metrics.name: Only surfaces visible at point of sale or during use must be disclosed
rubrics_metrics.description: Only those surfaces of the article that are visible at the point of sale or during use must be disclosed to meet 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b). The undisclosed surfaces not seen during sale or use are not required to be described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The drawing should illustrate the design as it will appear to purchasers and users since appearance is the basis for design patentability. The functionality need not be reproduced. If visible surfaces are flat and devoid of ornamentation, they need not be shown but should be described in the specification if they are considered part of the claimed design.

rubrics_metrics.name: When title defines entire article but drawings omit visible portions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications whose title defines an entire article but whose drawings/specification fail to disclose portions or surfaces of the article that would be visible either during use or on sale will not be considered to violate 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendment to the title will not be required. Examiners should include a statement in the first Office action indicating that the surface(s) or portion(s) of the article that would be normally visible but are not shown in the drawing or described in the specification are understood to form no part of the claimed design; form paragraph 15.85 may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiners must specifically identify drawing deficiencies for 35 U.S.C. 112 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: When a claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite due to an insufficient drawing disclosure, examiners must specifically identify in the Office action what the deficiencies are in the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A mere statement that the claim is nonenabling and indefinite due to poor drawing quality is insufficient. Examiners must specifically point out portions of the drawing that are insufficient to permit understanding of the shape and appearance and, if possible, suggest how the rejection may be overcome. Form paragraphs 15.21 and 15.20.02 may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistencies between drawing views
rubrics_metrics.description: When inconsistencies between the views of the drawings are so great that the overall appearance of the design is unclear, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Otherwise, inconsistencies between drawing views will be objected to by the examiner and correction required by the applicant. See MPEP § 1503.02. The Office action should specifically identify all inconsistencies when rejection is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poor-quality visual disclosure may render claim fatally defective
rubrics_metrics.description: If the visual disclosure of the claimed design as originally filed is of such poor quality that its overall shape and appearance cannot be understood, applicant should be advised that the claim might be fatally defective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 15.65 to advise applicant that claim may be fatally defective. Consider whether amendments or replacement drawing sheets can cure; if not, rejection may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative description limitations (no unsupportable broad language)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative description in the specification can supplement the drawing, but if the description refers to embodiments or modified forms not shown in the drawing, or includes vague words such as 'variations' and 'equivalents,' or states the claimed design is not limited to the exact shape and appearance shown, the claim should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) as nonenabling and indefinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such descriptive statements fail to enable a designer to make the other embodiments absent additional drawing views, and fail to particularly point out and distinctly claim the shape and appearance of those other embodiments. Form paragraph 15.21 may be used to reject on these grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undisclosed visible surface(s)/portion(s) do not form part of claimed design (15.85)
rubrics_metrics.description: The [1] of the article [2] not shown in the drawing or described in the specification. It is understood that the appearance of any part of the article not shown or described forms no part of the claimed design. Determination of patentability is based on the design shown and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 15.85 to indicate which visible surfaces/portions are not shown and thus not part of the claim; cite In re Zahn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment may not be possible (15.65)
rubrics_metrics.description: The application might be fatally defective because [1]. It might not be possible to identify any definite and enabled design claim without introducing new matter (35 U.S.C. 132, 37 CFR 1.121).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, identify the subject matter which is insufficiently disclosed. Use when drawing disclosure cannot be cured without adding new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrected drawing sheets required (15.73)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to submit replacement correction sheets overcoming all of the deficiencies in the drawing disclosure set forth above, or an explanation why the drawing corrections or additional drawing views are not necessary will result in the rejection of the claim under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b) being made FINAL in the next Office action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In bracket 1, insert surface or surfaces which are not shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: New matter objection under 35 U.S.C. 132 (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: New matter is subject matter which has no support in the original specification, drawings or claim. An amendment to the claim must have support in the original disclosure. Amendments introducing new matter must be objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior to final action, all amendments are entered and considered. To overcome objection, applicant may demonstrate by argument or evidence that original disclosure establishes possession of the amended subject matter. Form paragraph 15.51.01 may be used to object to new drawing/specification matter that lacks support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments affecting the claim must comply with written description (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: A design claim may be amended by broadening or narrowing its scope within the bounds of the disclosure as originally filed provided it complies with the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a). An amendment with no support introduces new matter and the claim must be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate any amendment that affects the claimed design for compliance with the written description requirement (see MPEP § 1504.04, subsection I.C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of amendments that introduce new matter (configuration or surface changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment changing the configuration of the original design (e.g., square seat to circular seat) or changing surface appearance by adding previously undisclosed three-dimensional surface treatment (beading, grooves, ribs) introduces new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such changes are departures from the original disclosure (see In re Salmon, In re Daniels). Removal of 3D surface treatment that was integral to configuration is a new-matter addition of underlying configuration. Conversely, removal of two-dimensional superimposed surface treatment may not introduce new matter if the underlying configuration was apparent from the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment converting solid/broken line structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting originally-disclosed solid lines to broken lines, or broken lines to solid lines, does not introduce new matter if such conversion does not introduce subject matter not originally disclosed; however, if such an amendment affects the claimed design the resulting design must be evaluated for written description compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Additional examples of amendments that would not introduce new matter include: (A) a preliminary amendment filed simultaneously with the application papers; and (B) inclusion of a disclaimer in the original specification or on the drawings/photographs as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶15.21 Rejection template for 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b)
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim is rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) and (b), or pre-AIA equivalents, as the claimed invention is not described in such full, clear, concise and exact terms as to enable any person skilled in the art to make and use the same, and fails to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the inventor regards as the invention. The claim is indefinite and nonenabling [1].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form paragraph should not be used when separate rejections under 112(a) and/or (b) are appropriate. In bracket 1, provide a complete explanation of the basis for the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶15.20.02 Suggestion: disclaiming indefinite/nonenabling areas via broken lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant may disclaim the areas or portions of the design which are considered indefinite and nonenabling in the rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112 above by converting them to broken lines and amending the specification to include a statement that the portions of the [1] shown in broken lines form no part of the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For international design applications, use form paragraph 29.27 instead. In bracket 1, insert title of the article. Use when conversion to broken lines can cure the deficiency without introducing new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: ¶15.51.01 Amendment to disclosure (not affecting claim) - 35 U.S.C. 132 objection
rubrics_metrics.description: The [1] is objected to under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 37 CFR 1.121 as introducing new matter. The original disclosure does not reasonably convey to a designer of ordinary skill that the inventor was in possession of the amended subject matter at the time the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specify whether new drawing or amendment to drawing, title or specification. Identify what is new matter so the basis for the objection is clear. To overcome, applicant may attempt to demonstrate (argument/evidence) that original disclosure establishes possession of amended subject matter, or provide specific corrective actions (e.g., omit broken-line environmental structure or amend title).
